newsitem.title: KENYA: IMF turns heat up on Kenya's Moi over corruption.
newsitem.headline: IMF turns heat up on Kenya's Moi over corruption.

text.p: The International Monetary Fund has turned up the heat on President Daniel arap Moi's government over corruption, forcing it to warn on Friday it would have to cut spending and probably raise taxes in an election year.
The IMF decision to halt a three-year aid programme worth $205 million cost Kenya much more than just that sum of money, it damaged its international credibility and scared foreign investors.
It also reminded some Kenyans of the grim atmosphere from 1991 to 1993 when donors froze aid to push Moi to agree to multi-party politics before he won the last general election.

The multi-million dollar question for many was whether Moi, 73, would buckle under to the IMF and take steps to bring to justice all the corrupt, even if they were hiding high in the government, or whether he would try to tough it out.

"The IMF have for the first time since 1991 the chance to get their way on this (corruption)," said a market analyst, who declined to be identified. "This is the only way to put pressure on the government."

"It's a blow to the ruling party, KANU, and if I was in their shoes I would ignore them, hold an election and then the IMF would only have to talk to KANU again. But the situation is not entirely under the control of the politicians," he added.
The analyst said much depended on whether the opposition capitalised on the IMF move and remained united in demanding reform despite government attempts to divide it again into squabbling factions.

The IMF move followed clashes in June and July between riot police and opposition-backed demonstrators demanding political reforms that pushed Moi to agree to some political changes before presidential and parliamentary polls later this year.
Opposition leaders have said they can only wait and see what reforms the Moi government will provide before judging them.
They have called for a nationwide general strike on August 8 to keep the government under pressure and push it to dialogue.
The IMF refused to accept promises any more and pulled the aid plug despite government assurances that an anti-graft authority would be set up and the energy sector cleaned up.
Foreign investors, diplomats and many Kenyan businessmen hoped it would force the president to tackle corruption once and for all and level the economic, as well as political, playing field.
But some opposition leaders said such hopes were far-fetched because for the government truly to move to root out corruption might require the removal of many of those near the top.

"I'm very pleased the IMF has finally recognised the enormous problem of governance in this country," said Richard Leakey, secretary-general of the unregistered Safina party, which campaigned for political reforms and against corruption.

"I sincerely hope the authorities in this country will take the appropriate response in terms of starting the process of reforms," he told Reuters, adding government attempts to pretend it was genuinely going to change had been shattered by the IMF.
First signals from the economic reform-minded finance minister were mixed. He said spending would be cut and revenues raised to cover some of the shortfall caused by the IMF move.
But he also sounded a conciliatory note, saying Kenya would open talks with the IMF on a "shadow" agreement, which would set goals for the government to meet before any aid was resumed.
"I sincerely hope the president and his government recognise that putting the burden of their bad government on the people is not going to win themy any votes in the future," Leakey said.

"What is needed is to sit down and discuss a way forward. A government of national unity and a commitment to constitutional reform would stop a shilling fall and very soon a government of national unity could restore some real confidence," he said.
